title: Sentence Correction

steps.title: Find the subject and verb
steps.content: A sentence needs a clear subject and a verb that agrees with it. Singular subjects usually take singular verbs; plural subjects take plural verbs.
steps.example: The student writes every day. / The students write every day.
steps.tip: Ignore extra phrases between the subject and verb when checking agreement.

steps.title: Subject–verb agreement
options: The list of items are on the desk.
The list of items is on the desk.
The lists of item is on the desk.
The list are on the desk.
steps.explanation: The subject is 'list' (singular). The phrase 'of items' does not change the subject, so use 'is'.
hints: Find the true subject, not the noun closest to the verb.
A singular subject generally takes a singular verb in the present simple; a plural subject takes a plural verb.

steps.title: Keep verb tense consistent
steps.content: Use the tense that matches the time of the action. Avoid switching between past and present without a reason.
steps.example: Incorrect: She entered the room and sits down. Correct: She entered the room and sat down.

steps.title: Choose the correct tense
steps.prompt: By the time we arrived, the meeting ___ .
options: starts
has started
had started
starting
steps.explanation: The meeting started before another past event (our arrival), so past perfect 'had started' is appropriate.
hints: Look for time markers such as yesterday, since, already or every day.
Make the verb tense match when the action happens and whether it continues.

steps.title: Pronouns and parallel structure
steps.content: A pronoun should clearly refer to a noun. Items in a list should use the same grammatical form (parallel structure).
steps.example: Parallel: The role requires planning, writing and presenting. Avoid mixing nouns and unrelated verb forms.

steps.title: Check parallel structure
steps.content: Items in a list or pair should use grammatically consistent forms. This is called parallel structure.
options: She enjoys coding, testing and documenting.
She enjoys coding, to test and documentation.
She enjoys to code, testing and document.
She enjoys code, test and documenting.
steps.explanation: Coding, testing and documenting are all gerunds, so the list uses a consistent grammatical form.
hints: Compare the grammatical form of each item in the list.
A list should keep verbs or nouns in a consistent structure.

steps.title: Correct subject–verb agreement
steps.content: A singular subject takes a singular verb in the present tense; a plural subject takes a plural verb. Do not let a nearby plural noun distract you from the actual subject.
steps.prompt: Complete the sentence: Each of the candidates ______ completed the assessment.
steps.explanation: Each is grammatically singular, so it takes has, not have.
hints: The phrase 'of the candidates' does not change the number of the subject.

steps.title: Proofread a sentence systematically
steps.content: A reliable correction process checks sentence structure before minor style choices.
options: Check punctuation and word choice
Find the subject and main verb
Check agreement and tense
Read the complete sentence for meaning
steps.explanation: Identify the core subject and verb, check agreement and tense, then review punctuation and word choice and reread the complete sentence.
hints: Start with the main grammatical structure.
Read the corrected sentence as a whole to make sure the intended meaning remains clear.

options: Each of the players have a jersey.
Each of the players has a jersey.
Each players has a jersey.
Each of players have a jersey.

questions.prompt: Neither the manager nor the employees ___ available.
options: is
was
are
be
questions.explanation: With 'neither…nor', the verb commonly agrees with the nearer subject; 'employees' is plural.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence with consistent tense.
options: He opened the door and walks in.
He opens the door and walked in.
He opened the door and walked in.
He opening the door and walked in.
questions.explanation: Both actions are completed in the past, so both verbs use past tense.

options: She likes reading, writing and to swim.
She likes to read, writing and swimming.
She likes reading, writing and swimming.
She likes read, writing and swim.
questions.explanation: All three items are gerunds: reading, writing and swimming.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct article: She is ___ honest engineer.
options: a
an
the
no article
questions.explanation: 'Honest' begins with a vowel sound because the h is silent, so use 'an'.

learning_objectives: Identify subjects, verbs and agreement relationships.
Correct common tense and pronoun errors.
Use parallel structure in lists and paired expressions.
Apply articles, prepositions and punctuation in context.
Proofread a sentence without changing its intended meaning.

common_misconceptions.misconception: The noun closest to the verb always determines agreement.
common_misconceptions.correction: Find the grammatical subject; intervening phrases do not change its number.

common_misconceptions.misconception: A list sounds acceptable even when its grammatical forms differ.
common_misconceptions.correction: Parallel items should follow a consistent grammatical structure.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Grammar correction means replacing a sentence with a more complicated one.
common_misconceptions.correction: Preserve the original meaning and make only the changes needed for correctness and clarity.

worked_examples.title: Find the real subject
worked_examples.input: The list of selected candidates is ready.
trace: The phrase 'of selected candidates' describes the list.
List is singular, so use is.
worked_examples.explanation: Do not let a nearby plural noun control the verb.

worked_examples.title: Repair parallel structure
worked_examples.input: The role requires coding, testing and to document changes.
trace: The first item is a gerund: coding.
The second item is a gerund: testing.
Make the third item a gerund too: documenting.
worked_examples.explanation: Consistent grammatical forms make lists easier to read.

worked_examples.title: Keep tense consistent
worked_examples.input: Yesterday she reviewed the code and fixes the bug.
trace: The first verb reviewed is past tense.
The second verb fixes is present tense.
Use fixed to keep the completed past actions consistent.
worked_examples.output: Yesterday she reviewed the code and fixed the bug.
worked_examples.explanation: Tense should reflect the time relationship between actions.

company_applications.practice: Find subject–verb agreement errors and choose a grammatically correct rewrite.
Correct tense, pronoun and parallel-structure mistakes.
Improve clarity without changing the sentence's intended meaning.

srs_cards.question: What determines subject–verb agreement?
srs_cards.answer: The grammatical subject, not a nearby noun inside a descriptive phrase.

srs_cards.question: What is parallel structure?
srs_cards.answer: Using consistent grammatical forms for items in a list or paired construction.

srs_cards.question: What is a reliable first step in sentence correction?
srs_cards.answer: Identify the subject and main verb, then check agreement and tense.

quest.story: A hiring communication test contains messages with subtle agreement, tense and structure errors. Your task is to make each sentence clear without changing what the writer intended.
quest.mission: Diagnose the grammar rule, correct the sentence and explain why the original construction fails.
success_criteria: Find the real subject and verb.
